title: Module 5 · Lesson 2 — Task decomposition, planning and replanning

lines: Module Five, Lesson Two: planning and replanning.
How an agent turns a goal into steps, and knows when to change course.
Picture an agent organizing a three-day team offsite in Lisbon for twelve people.
Flights, a hotel, a meeting room, and an agenda, all within budget.
Planning turns that goal into a sequence of steps that respects dependencies.
Just as important, it notices when the plan stops being valid.
A usable step runs on its own, can be verified, and is the right size.
For every step, ask: how would I know this succeeded?
Split too finely, and twenty tiny steps cost more to coordinate than the work.
Split too coarsely, and one giant step can't be done in a single action.
Dependencies decide the shape of the run.
Flights, hotel, and venue don't depend on each other, so they run at the same time.
That concurrency is the whole case for Plan and Execute over ReAct.
Drawn as a graph, total time is the critical path, not the sum of every step.

say.0: That concurrency is the whole case for Plan and Execute over Ree-Act.

lines: A plan is a hypothesis, so name what breaks it.
A step fails after its retries, like a hotel that stays fully booked.
A result contradicts an assumption, like a venue that seats only ten.
Or new information makes steps unnecessary, so stop instead of running them out of momentum.
The budget no longer covers the rest of the plan.
Or the user changes the goal mid-run, and the offsite moves to Porto.
Unbounded replanning is just a loop with extra steps.
Cap the replans, make each plan meaningfully different, and escalate to a human at the cap.
Planning is the highest-leverage call, so use your strongest model to plan.
A cheaper model can carry out the steps.
A bad plan cannot be rescued by good execution.
But a mediocre executor following a good plan usually still succeeds.
Expect an exam question on when to replan, and remember that a step going as expected is not a trigger.
Read on for the full list, and a plan written as a graph.
